questions.question: A monthly budget table is written out in words with four rows. Income row: allowance $80 for the month. Fixed expenses row: bus pass $28. Variable expenses row: snacks $6 each week, for 4 weeks in the month. Savings row: $16 put into a savings account. What is the total of the expense side (fixed + variable + saving)?
questions.explain: Turn the weekly snack money into a monthly amount first ($6 x 4 = $24), then add every row on the expense side, including saving: $28 + $24 + $16 = $68. The most common trap is leaving the $16 saving out and answering $52 — saving is money you assign, so it belongs on the expense side of the budget.

questions.question: A monthly budget table is written out in words. Income row: $120 from babysitting. Fixed expenses rows: phone plan $20 and bus pass $30. Variable expenses row: swim drop-in $6 each week, for 4 weeks. Savings row: $22. Does this budget balance?
options: No — expenses total $78, leaving $42 unassigned
No — expenses total $96, leaving $24 unassigned
No — expenses total $74, leaving $46 unassigned
Yes — income and expenses both come to $120 here
questions.explain: Make the swim cost monthly ($6 x 4 = $24), add all four expense rows ($20 + $30 + $24 + $22 = $96), then compare with the $120 income: $24 has no job yet, so it does not balance. A budget balances only when the two sides are equal, not when income is merely big enough.

questions.question: A monthly budget table is written out in words. Income row: $150. Fixed expenses row: $62. Variable expenses row: lunches $12 each week, for 4 weeks. Savings row: left blank. What amount goes in the savings row so the budget balances?
options: $110, which is what the two expense rows add to
$76, using the $12 lunch amount just one time
$40, so the expense side also totals $150
$0, since saving is not an expense-side row
questions.explain: Change lunches to a monthly amount ($12 x 4 = $48), add the spending rows ($62 + $48 = $110), then subtract from income: $150 - $110 = $40 for saving. Writing $110 in the savings row is the usual slip — that number is the spending total, not the leftover.

questions.question: A monthly budget table is written out in words. Income row: $95 from dog walking. Fixed expenses rows: bus pass $30 and phone $25. Variable expenses row: snacks $6 each week, for 4 weeks. Savings row: $30. Which statement about this budget is true?
options: It has $4 left over, so a bit more can be saved
It has $16 left over after the four rows add up
It balances, since income and expenses both are $95
It is short by $14, so one row must drop by $14
questions.explain: Snacks are $6 x 4 = $24 per month, so the expense side is $30 + $25 + $24 + $30 = $109, which is $14 more than the $95 income. Using $6 instead of $24 makes the budget look nearly balanced — always convert weekly amounts to monthly before you compare the two sides.

questions.question: A monthly budget has income $240, fixed expenses $95, variable expenses of $17 each week for 4 weeks, and saving $60. How much of the income is left unassigned?
questions.explain: Variable costs are $17 x 4 = $68, so the whole expense side is $95 + $68 + $60 = $223, and $240 - $223 = $17 is unassigned. Answering $77 means the $60 saving was left off the expense side, which always makes the leftover look too big.

questions.question: A monthly budget shows income $300 with fixed expenses $140, variable expenses $85 and saving $95, so the expense side comes to $320. Which single change makes the budget balance?
options: Move $20 from the fixed row into the saving row
Lower the variable row from $85 down to $65
Take out the $95 saving, as saving is not spending
Raise the income row by $20 to match the $320
questions.explain: The expense side is $20 too big, so shrink an expense row by $20: $85 - $20 = $65 makes the expense side $300, equal to the income. Moving money between two expense rows keeps the total at $320, and you cannot raise the income row unless you actually earn more.

questions.question: A monthly budget is to balance exactly. Fixed expenses are $210, variable expenses are $36 each week for 4 weeks, and saving is $86. What monthly income is needed?
questions.explain: Add the full expense side — $210 + ($36 x 4) + $86 = $440 — because a balanced budget has income equal to everything assigned, saving included. Leaving the $86 saving out gives $354, and using $36 only once gives $332.

questions.question: Nadia budgets a month with income $180. Her fixed expenses are a bus pass $32 and guitar lessons $60, and her variable expense is bubble tea at $7 each week for 4 weeks. Everything left goes to saving. How much can she save?
options: $0, because saving is not an expense row
$81, using the $7 bubble tea amount once
$120, which is what the three rows add to
$60, so the expense side totals $180
questions.explain: Bubble tea is $7 x 4 = $28 monthly, so the spending rows are $32 + $60 + $28 = $120 and saving takes the rest: $180 - $120 = $60. Forgetting to multiply the weekly amount by 4 leaves too much room and gives $81.

questions.question: Ravi earns $22 every Saturday walking dogs, and this month has 4 Saturdays. He also received a one-time $95 birthday gift. His fixed expenses are phone $35 and transit pass $28, and his variable spending is $46. He wants the budget to balance with all the rest going into his savings account. How much goes to saving?
options: $74, from $183 of income minus $109 of costs
$8, from $117 of income minus the $109 of costs
$109, the amount the three expense rows add to
$183, because saving is what the income row holds
questions.explain: Turn the weekly earnings into a monthly amount ($22 x 4 = $88), add the one-time gift for income of $183, subtract the spending rows ($35 + $28 + $46 = $109), and save the $74 that is left. The classic trap is adding one $22 Saturday to the $95 gift, which mixes a weekly amount with a monthly one.

questions.question: Maya's monthly budget balanced last month: income $260, fixed expenses $120, variable expenses $80, saving $60. This month her bus pass goes up by $15. She keeps the same $260 income and still wants to save $60. What must she do so the budget balances again?
options: Add $15 to the income row so the sides match
Cut the variable row from $80 down to $65
Move $15 from saving into the variable row
Leave it — the $60 saving covers the extra $15
questions.explain: Fixed expenses become $135, so with income $260 and saving fixed at $60, the variable row must be $260 - $135 - $60 = $65, a cut of $15. Shifting money between two expense rows leaves the expense total at $275, so the budget still does not balance.

questions.question: Ellie's monthly budget lists income $45 from babysitting, phone $18, snacks $3 each week for 4 weeks, and saving $8. She writes: “Expenses $38, income $45 — my budget is balanced.” What is really going on?
options: Her total is wrong: the expense side is really $29
Her total is wrong: saving does not belong there
Her total is right, but $7 is still unassigned
Nothing is wrong: $45 of income covers the $38
questions.explain: Her expense side is correct — $18 + ($3 x 4) + $8 = $38 — but $45 is not $38, so $7 of income has no job and the budget does not balance yet. Having enough income is not the same as balancing; assign the extra $7 to a row, such as saving.

questions.question: Theo's monthly income is a $110 allowance plus $16 each week from a paper route, with 4 weeks this month. His fixed expenses are phone $30 and transit $25, and he wants $50 to go into his savings account. The rest becomes his variable spending money. What variable amount makes the budget balance?
options: $21, from $126 of income after the other rows
$105, which is what the other rows add up to
$119, since the $50 saving is not an expense
$69, so the expense side also totals $174
questions.explain: Income is $110 + ($16 x 4) = $174, and the other assigned rows come to $30 + $25 + $50 = $105, leaving $174 - $105 = $69 for variable spending. Two traps hide here: adding just one $16 week to the allowance, and skipping the $50 saving because it does not feel like spending.
